# Orientation: computers and where you compute {#sec-orientation}

**Core.** Work through it, with the exercises.

::: {.callout-note .goals icon=false}
## Learning goals

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

1. Open a terminal on your computer and run a command you were given.
2. Download a FASTQ file, check that it arrived intact, look at its first
   records, and count its reads.
3. Find how many logical CPUs, how much RAM, and how much free disk your
   computer has.
4. Estimate a file's size from its read count, and name the resources
   (CPU, RAM, disk, I/O) a job can be limited by.
5. Decide whether a job belongs on a laptop, a cluster, or the cloud.
:::

## What this chapter does {#sec-orientation-intro}

By the end of this chapter you will have run your first commands on a real
sequencing file: you will download it, check it, look inside it, and count
its reads. Then we step back and look at the machine that did the work, and
at the other machines you will use.

In bioinformatics, "the computer" is usually not the one in front of you. It
is most often someone else's Linux machine, such as a university or USDA
cluster, that you reach from your laptop. Your laptop is still where you
edit, look at results, and run small analyses. This chapter starts on the
laptop, because that is where everything begins.

## Opening a terminal {#sec-orientation-terminal}

Three words first. The **operating system** is the software that runs the
computer: macOS, Windows, or Linux. The **terminal** is a window where you
type commands. The **shell** is the program inside that window that reads
each command, runs it, and prints the result.

Opening a terminal is the one step that really differs between systems.
Pick yours; every other tabbed box on this page will follow your choice.

::: {.panel-tabset group="os"}
## macOS

Open **Terminal**: press {{< kbd Cmd-Space >}}, type `Terminal`, and press
{{< kbd Return >}}. (It lives in *Applications → Utilities*.)

The shell on a Mac is **zsh**. Every command in this chapter works in zsh.
@sec-shell-basics introduces bash, the shell on most clusters, without changing
your Mac's settings.

You may read about [Homebrew](https://brew.sh), a popular way to install
command-line tools on a Mac. You do not need it for this book: @sec-book-setup
sets up every tool with pixi.

## Windows (WSL2)

Windows does not run the book's commands directly. Instead you install
**WSL2** (Windows Subsystem for Linux), which runs a real Ubuntu Linux system
inside Windows. This takes longer than on the other systems: an install, a
restart, and creating a Linux account. Allow 20–30 minutes.

1. Open **PowerShell as administrator**: open the Start menu, type
   `PowerShell`, right-click *Windows PowerShell*, and choose *Run as
   administrator*.
2. Run this one command, which installs WSL2 with Ubuntu:

   ```{.powershell filename="PowerShell (laptop, as administrator)"}
   wsl --install
   ```

3. Restart Windows when it asks.
4. Open **Ubuntu** from the Start menu. The first time, it asks you to make
   a Linux user name and password. **Nothing appears while you type the
   password**: no dots, no stars. That is normal. Type it, press
   {{< kbd Enter >}}, and type it again.

From now on, every command in this book runs in the Ubuntu window, not in
PowerShell. Its shell is **bash**.

If the install is blocked, your laptop may be managed by your university;
ask your IT office. Microsoft's [WSL install
guide](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install) has the
current official steps [@microsoft2025install]. You may also have heard of
Git Bash; it is a different tool, and this book does not support it.

## Linux

You already have a terminal. On Ubuntu, press {{< kbd Ctrl-Alt-T >}}; on
other distributions, look for *Terminal* in the applications menu. The
shell is usually **bash**.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: Windows folders from WSL

In WSL, keep your work in your Linux home folder (`~`), not under
`/mnt/c/...`, where Linux sees your Windows files. Windows folders are slow
to use from Linux and invite line-ending and permission problems
([Microsoft's advice](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/filesystems)).
:::

@tbl-terminal-by-os sums up what you now have.

: What you type commands into, by operating system. {#tbl-terminal-by-os}

| Operating system | Terminal app | Default shell | Supported in this book |
|:-----------------|:-------------|:--------------|:-----------------------|
| macOS | Terminal | zsh | yes |
| Windows | Ubuntu (WSL2) | bash | yes |
| Windows | PowerShell, Git Bash | — | no |
| Linux (e.g., Ubuntu) | Terminal | bash (usually) | yes |

The terminal shows a **prompt**: a short line ending in `$` (bash) or `%`
(zsh), often with your user name and folder in front. It means "ready for a
command". Code blocks in this book leave the prompt out, so you can copy and
paste them as they are. Each block is labelled with where it runs; in this
chapter that is always `Terminal (laptop)`.

## Guided first session {#sec-orientation-first-session}

Now run some commands. Copy each one, paste it into your terminal, press
{{< kbd Enter >}}, and compare what you see with the output shown below it.
You do not need to understand every part yet: you will learn these commands
properly in Part II. Seeing them work first makes that easier.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Pasting into a terminal

Paste with {{< kbd Cmd-V >}} on macOS and {{< kbd Ctrl-Shift-V >}} in most
Linux and WSL terminals. In a terminal, {{< kbd Ctrl-C >}} does *not* copy:
it stops the running command.
:::

The file we use holds yeast (*Saccharomyces cerevisiae*) RNA-seq reads from
an experiment by @wu2018repression, cut down to 50,000 reads by the nf-core
project for testing. It is the running dataset of this book; its source and
license are listed in the book's `data/README.md`.

**Step 1. Make a scratch folder and move into it.**

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
mkdir -p ~/bioinf-ch01 && cd ~/bioinf-ch01
```

This prints nothing. In the shell, silence usually means success.

**Step 2. Download one FASTQ file.**

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
curl -fLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/test-datasets/rnaseq/testdata/GSE110004/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
```

`curl` shows a progress table while it works. When it finishes, the last
line starts with `100`; your speeds and times will differ:

```{.console}
  % Total    % Received % Xferd  Average Speed   Time    Time     Time  Current
                                 Dload  Upload   Total   Spent    Left  Speed
100 2186k  100 2186k    0     0  4146k      0 --:--:-- --:--:-- --:--:-- 4141k
```

If instead you see `curl: (56) The requested URL returned error: 404`, or
any other `curl:` error, check that you copied the whole command. If a
firewall blocks `curl`, download the file in your browser from its [GitHub
page](https://github.com/nf-core/test-datasets/blob/rnaseq/testdata/GSE110004/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz)
(the *Download raw file* button), then move it into place:

::: {.panel-tabset group="os"}
## macOS
```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
mv ~/Downloads/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz ~/bioinf-ch01/
```
## Windows (WSL2)
Replace `<your-windows-name>` with your Windows user name.

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
cp /mnt/c/Users/<your-windows-name>/Downloads/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz ~/bioinf-ch01/
```
## Linux
```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
mv ~/Downloads/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz ~/bioinf-ch01/
```
:::

**Step 3. Check that the file arrived intact.** First its size:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
ls -lh SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
```

```{.console}
-rw-r--r--  1 you  staff   2.1M Nov 13 11:52 SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
```

Your name, group, and date will differ. The size shows as `2.1M` on macOS
and `2.2M` on Linux and WSL; the next section explains why. Then test the
compression:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gzip -t SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
```

This prints nothing if the file is intact. A damaged or incomplete
download prints an error instead.

**Step 4. Look at the first two reads.** The file is compressed
(`.gz`), so we decompress it on the fly and show only its first 8 lines:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | head -n 8
```

```{.console}
@SRR6357070.25017281 25017281/1 kraken:taxid|4932
CCTGAATCGAGAAGGAGGTGTCCAGGGAGTTCATCATCAGAATGATTAGTATGATTTACTGTAGATTCAGTAAGTTTCTGGCCTAAGATGAAGGTCGTGCT
+
BBBBBFFFFFFFBFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFBFFFBFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFBFFBFFFFFFF
@SRR6357070.6710070 6710070/1 kraken:taxid|4932
GTCAGATTGGAAGTCATGGTCAGATTCTATGTTAAGATCATCGGATTGTTGGATCTCATTTGACGCAATGAACGATTGATATGAAGCAGTTAAACGGTTTA
+
BBBBBFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFB
```

We use `gunzip -c` because it works the same on every system. (You may see
`zcat` elsewhere; on macOS it does not read `.gz` files.)

**Step 5. Count the lines.**

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
gunzip -c SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | wc -l
```

```{.console}
  200000
```

Linux and WSL print it without the leading spaces.

**Step 6. Count the reads and save the result.** Each read in this file
takes four lines, as you saw in step 4, so 200,000 lines are
200,000 / 4 = 50,000 reads. This command does the same count, divides by
4, and writes one line to a file:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
echo "SRR6357070_1 reads: $(( $(gunzip -c SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | wc -l) / 4 ))" > fastq_summary.txt # <1>
cat fastq_summary.txt                                                                                # <2>
```
1. `$( ... )` runs the line count from step 5 and puts its result here;
   `$(( ... / 4 ))` divides it by 4; `echo` prints the sentence; and `>`
   sends that sentence into the file `fastq_summary.txt` instead of the
   screen.
2. `cat` prints the file, so you can check what was saved.

```{.console}
SRR6357070_1 reads: 50000
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: stop at the first error

If any step prints an error, stop and fix it before going on. In
particular, a summary that says `reads: 0` means the download failed or the
file is broken; the command still "succeeds", because the shell does not
stop on errors unless told to (@sec-shell-scripts).
:::

You now have a one-line summary of a real sequencing file. Before moving
on, look at what a read is. @fig-fastq-record labels the first record from
step 4.

::: {#fig-fastq-record}
{{< svg ../figures/fastq-record.svg >}}

The first record of `SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz`. In this file every read takes
exactly four lines: a header with the read ID, the bases, a `+`
separator, and one quality character per base. The full format, including
files that break the four-line pattern, is in @sec-fasta-fastq.
:::

`~/bioinf-ch01` is a scratch folder: you can delete it whenever you like.
@sec-organizing-projects starts the book's real project and brings this file, and the
address you downloaded it from, into it.

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** This FASTQ file has 200,000 lines. How many reads does
it hold?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
50,000. In this file each read takes four lines, so 200,000 / 4 = 50,000.
:::
:::

## Parts of a computer that matter for analysis {#sec-orientation-parts}

Start with your own computer. Run the commands for your system and write
your values in the last column of @tbl-my-computer.

: The resources of one computer. macOS uses different commands for CPUs
and RAM; all commands are in the tabs below. The example values are from
one laptop (a Mac); yours will differ. {#tbl-my-computer}

| Resource | Command (Linux / WSL) | Read this | Example output | Your value |
|:---------|:----------------------|:----------|:---------------|:-----------|
| Logical CPUs | `nproc` | the number | `16` | |
| RAM | `free -h` | `total` in the `Mem:` row | `68 GB` | |
| Free disk | `df -h ~` | the `Avail` column | `744Gi` | |

::: {.panel-tabset group="os"}
## macOS
```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
sysctl -n hw.ncpu
echo "$(( $(sysctl -n hw.memsize) / 1000000000 )) GB"
df -h ~
```

```{.console}
16
68 GB
Filesystem      Size    Used   Avail Capacity iused ifree %iused  Mounted on
/dev/disk1s1   1.8Ti   1.1Ti   744Gi    60%    6.1M  7.8G    0%   /System/Volumes/Data
```

Read free disk from the `Avail` column. On a Mac, `Used` and `Avail` need
not add up to `Size`, because several volumes share one disk.

## Windows (WSL2)
```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
nproc
free -h
df -h ~
```

For RAM, read the `total` column of the `Mem:` row of `free -h`; for disk,
the `Avail` column of `df -h ~`. WSL sees only the memory Windows gives its
virtual machine, by default about half the laptop's RAM, not the full
amount ([WSL settings](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/wsl-config)).

## Linux
```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
nproc
free -h
df -h ~
```

For RAM, read the `total` column of the `Mem:` row of `free -h`; for disk,
the `Avail` column of `df -h ~`.
:::

These three numbers describe the parts in @fig-computer-parts:

- **CPU** (central processing unit): the part that computes. It has
  several **physical cores**, each able to work on its own. On many Intel
  and AMD processors, each core appears to the system as two **logical
  CPUs**; the commands above count logical CPUs. (The example laptop has 8
  physical cores and 16 logical CPUs.) A running program splits its work
  into **threads**, pieces of work that the system places onto CPUs. Many
  tools take an option that sets how many threads to use: `--threads`,
  `-t`, or `-p`, depending on the tool. More threads help only if the tool
  is written to use them.
- **RAM** (memory): the fast working space a program uses while it runs.
  It is emptied when the program stops.
- **Disk** (storage): slow, large, and permanent; it keeps your files. A
  file's size on disk is not the RAM a program needs to read it. The count
  in step 6 *streams* through the file a few lines at a time and needs
  almost no memory, whatever the file's size. Other tools, such as those
  that build a genome index (@sec-indexing-genomes), hold a lot in memory at once.
- **I/O** (input/output): reading and writing files, over the disk or the
  network. Simple steps over big files, such as counting or compressing,
  often spend most of their time waiting for I/O. Heavier steps, such as
  aligning reads, are often limited by the CPU, and some by RAM.

::: {#fig-computer-parts}
{{< svg ../figures/computer-parts.svg >}}

The parts of a computer that matter for analysis, fastest on the left.
Speeds are typical laptop values, order of magnitude only. Shown is one
example, an I/O-limited job: blocks of the file crawl from disk into RAM
while the CPU's cores wait.
:::

@fig-cores-threads shows what threads do, and do not do, on a computer with
8 cores.

::: {#fig-cores-threads}
{{< svg ../figures/cores-threads.svg >}}

Threads on a computer with 8 cores. Left: a tool written to use threads,
run with 4, keeps 4 cores busy. Right: a single-threaded step keeps 1 core
busy and leaves 7 idle; asking it for more threads changes nothing.
:::

::: {.callout-caution .misconception}
## Misconception: "More cores always makes it faster"
**Reality.** Only steps written to use several threads get faster, and only
until something else limits them. Many steps use one core, and some are
limited by disk, network, or memory rather than the CPU.
:::

Each resource fails in its own way when it runs out (@tbl-resource-limits).
You will meet these messages; recognising them saves hours.

: What it looks like when each resource runs out. {#tbl-resource-limits}

| Resource | What runs out | What you see |
|:---------|:--------------|:-------------|
| RAM | Working space while the program runs | The program stops with `Killed` or an "out of memory" message, often with no output file |
| Disk | Space to write files | `No space left on device` |
| CPU | Computing power | The job is slow; its cores show 100% busy |
| I/O | Speed of reading and writing | The job is slow, but its cores are mostly idle |

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
A job can be limited by CPU, RAM, disk space, or I/O. Extra cores help only
when the work can use them.
:::

Finding which one limits a real job is part of @sec-hpc-slurm (on a cluster)
and @sec-performance.

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** A step keeps one core at 100% while seven sit idle.
Will rerunning it with `--threads 8` make it faster?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
Only if the tool supports threads. Many steps use one core whatever you
ask for, and then nothing changes. Some are limited by disk or memory, not
the CPU, and more threads will not help those either.
:::
:::

## How big is the data? {#sec-orientation-data-sizes}

Start with your own file. It holds 50,000 reads and takes 2.2 MB
compressed (12.8 MB uncompressed). A typical RNA-seq sample has around 30
million reads in each mate file, 600 times as many. If those reads are like
ours, the file is about 600 times larger:

- compressed: 2.2 MB × 600 ≈ 1.3 GB
- uncompressed: 12.8 MB × 600 ≈ 7.7 GB

A paired-end sample has two such files, one for read 1 (`_1`) and one for
read 2 (`_2`). Our sample is paired too: your file holds 50,000 reads, and
its mate file `SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz` holds another 50,000, so the sample is
50,000 read *pairs* (100,000 reads).

This kind of scaling works only for the same kind of file. Read length,
header style, and compression all change the result, so treat it as an
estimate.

A note on units: in this book, 1 MB is 1,000,000 bytes and 1 GB is
1,000,000,000 bytes. Some tools count in powers of 2 instead
(1 MiB = 1,048,576 bytes) and often still print `M`. `ls -lh` is one of
them: your 2,239,317-byte file is 2.14 MiB, which macOS shows as `2.1M`
and Linux, which always rounds up, as `2.2M`.

Files later in a pipeline fall into two groups (@tbl-data-sizes,
@fig-pipeline-file-sizes):

- **Read-level files** (FASTQ, BAM) hold every read: gigabytes per sample in
  a real study. A BAM file holds the same reads placed on the genome, and
  is often about as large as the compressed FASTQ files it came from,
  sometimes larger. Sorting it needs temporary disk space on top
  ([`samtools sort`](https://www.htslib.org/doc/samtools-sort.html)).
- **Summary files** (count matrix, results table, and in DNA studies often a
  VCF of variants) hold one row per gene or variant: megabytes or less for
  RNA-seq, small enough for any laptop.

::: {.wide-table}
| Format | What it holds | Group | Yeast test set (measured) | Typical study |
|:-------|:--------------|:------|:--------------------------|:--------------|
| FASTQ (`.fastq.gz`) | Every read, with a quality per base | read-level | 2.2 MB per mate file; 4.3 MB for one paired sample | about 1 GB per mate file; a few GB per sample |
| BAM (`.bam`) | Every read, placed on the genome | read-level | 3.3 MB for one sample | a few GB per sample |
| Count matrix | One count per gene per sample | summary | 2.8 kB (124 genes × 5 samples) | a few MB for the whole study |
| Results table | One row per gene: fold change, p-value | summary | 12.7 kB (124 genes) | a few MB |
| VCF (`.vcf.gz`, DNA studies) | One row per variant | summary | none (RNA-seq) | MB for a few samples; GB for large cohorts |

: File sizes in an RNA-seq analysis. The yeast test set is measured; it
uses only yeast chromosome I, which is why it has 124 genes. A whole yeast
genome has about 6,000 genes and a mammal 20,000 or more. The typical
study column is a rough order of magnitude. {#tbl-data-sizes}
:::

::: {#fig-pipeline-file-sizes}
{{< svg ../figures/pipeline-file-sizes.svg >}}

Measured file sizes along the pipeline for the yeast test data, on a log
scale. The sample is `WT_REP2`, one paired run like yours (50,000 read
pairs). The BAM is the nf-core/rnaseq output stored with the test data;
the count matrix and results table were made from those BAMs by
`scripts/ch01_file_sizes.R`. Read-level files are hundreds to thousands of
times larger than summary files.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea
Read-level files (FASTQ, BAM) are large; summary files (count matrices,
results tables) are usually far smaller. Intermediate and temporary files
raise the peak disk space a pipeline needs.
:::

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** Our mate file holds 50,000 reads in 2.2 MB. About how
large is a mate file of the same kind with 30 million reads?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
About 1.3 GB compressed: 30 million is 600 × 50,000, and
600 × 2.2 MB ≈ 1.3 GB. A paired sample has two such files.
:::
:::

## Why Linux {#sec-orientation-linux}

Almost every cluster runs Linux, and most bioinformatics tools are written
for it first. That is why this book teaches Linux commands. macOS is close
enough that nearly all of them work unchanged, and WSL gives Windows a real
Linux system. Where macOS or Windows differ, the book says so.

::: {.callout-note}
## Background: Linux distributions
Linux comes in *distributions* that share the same core and commands but
differ in how software is installed. You will most often meet
[Ubuntu](https://ubuntu.com) on laptops and WSL, and Red Hat Enterprise
Linux or [Rocky Linux](https://rockylinux.org) on clusters.
:::

## Where you compute: laptop, cluster, cloud {#sec-orientation-where}

You will use up to three kinds of computer (@tbl-where-compute).

: Three places to compute. {#tbl-where-compute}

| | Laptop | Cluster (HPC) | Cloud |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Cost to you | already paid for | usually free or cheap through your institution | pay for each hour used and each GB stored |
| Size | a few to ~16 cores; 8–64 GB RAM | thousands of cores; nodes with hundreds of GB of RAM | as large as you pay for |
| Who manages it | you | research computing staff | you, on the provider's machines |
| What to run there | editing, plots, R and Python on summary files, small tests | alignment, many samples, pipelines, large-memory jobs | work your cluster cannot do, or when you have no cluster |

A **cluster**, or HPC (high-performance computing) system, is many
computers, called **nodes**, shared by many people (@fig-cluster-anatomy).
You connect from your laptop to a **login node**. There you edit files and
**submit jobs**: requests for some cores, memory, and time. A program called
the **scheduler** holds each job in a queue until those resources are free,
then runs it on a **compute node**. Your files sit on shared storage, which
both the login node and the compute nodes can read. @sec-working-remotely covers
connecting and @sec-hpc-slurm the scheduler.

::: {#fig-cluster-anatomy}
{{< svg ../figures/cluster-anatomy.svg >}}

The parts of an HPC cluster. You reach the login node from your laptop with
`ssh`; work runs on compute nodes when the scheduler starts it; shared
storage is connected to both. Files do not pass through the scheduler.
:::

::: {.callout-caution .misconception}
## Misconception: "The cluster is just a faster computer"
**Reality.** A cluster is many ordinary computers shared by many people.
You ask a scheduler for cores, memory, and time, and your job waits in a
queue until they are free. A single step is often no faster than on a
laptop; the gain is running many steps at once, with more memory.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall: heavy work on the login node
The login node is a shared doorway. Running an analysis there slows it for
everyone, and many sites kill long-running processes on it. The commands
in this chapter would work on a login node, but real analysis always runs
on compute nodes, as a job (@sec-hpc-slurm).
:::

The **cloud** is computers you rent by the hour from a company. It costs
money for every hour and every gigabyte, so for most readers it is the
option for when a cluster cannot do the job. @sec-cloud introduces it.

::: {.check}
**Check yourself.** Laptop, cluster, or cloud?

1. Editing an analysis script.
2. Aligning the reads of 48 samples.
3. Running DESeq2 on this book's small yeast count matrix.
4. A one-off job that needs 2 TB of RAM, more than any node of your
   cluster has.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
1. Laptop (or the login node, if the script lives on the cluster).
2. Cluster compute nodes, submitted as jobs.
3. Laptop: the matrix is a few kilobytes.
4. The cloud is one option if you have funding for it; another is a shared
   facility that has such nodes.
:::
:::

## Getting a cluster account {#sec-orientation-account}

Most readers will need a cluster account for the later chapters. Apply
early, since approval can take days or weeks. Ask your PI or your
institution's research computing office which cluster you can use.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Apply for an account now
ARS scientists and their collaborators can [sign up for
SCINet](https://scinet.usda.gov/about/signup), USDA's clusters. Universities
run their own, such as [Iowa State's HPC
clusters](https://www.hpc.iastate.edu/) (Nova). Step-by-step details are in
@sec-cluster-sites.
:::

No cluster yet? Keep going: everything up to @sec-working-remotely runs on your laptop.

## Summary {#sec-orientation-summary}

- A terminal runs a shell (zsh on macOS, bash on Linux and WSL); you type
  commands, and code blocks in this book leave out the prompt and say where
  they run.
- You downloaded a FASTQ file, checked it, looked at its records, and saved
  a read count: `SRR6357070_1 reads: 50000`.
- Your computer's logical CPUs, RAM, and free disk are three commands away;
  a job can be limited by CPU, RAM, disk, or I/O, and more threads help only
  tools written to use them.
- Read-level files (FASTQ, BAM) are large; summary files (count matrices,
  results) are small. File size scales with read count for files of the
  same kind.
- Edit and run small analyses on a laptop; run heavy jobs on cluster compute
  nodes, never on the login node; rent the cloud when neither will do.

## Exercises {#sec-orientation-exercises}

::: {.check}
**Exercise 1. Read 2.** Download the matching read-2 file and add its count
as a second line of `fastq_summary.txt`:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
curl -fLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/test-datasets/rnaseq/testdata/GSE110004/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
echo "SRR6357070_2 reads: $(( $(gunzip -c SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz | wc -l) / 4 ))" >> fastq_summary.txt
cat fastq_summary.txt
```

The only change from step 6 is `>>` instead of `>`: `>` replaces a file's
contents, `>>` adds to the end (@sec-text-tools). Do both files have the same
count? Why should they?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer

```{.console}
SRR6357070_1 reads: 50000
SRR6357070_2 reads: 50000
```

Yes. In a paired-end run each fragment is read from both ends, so read 1
and read 2 of a pair sit at the same position in the two files, and the
counts must match. Equal counts do not by themselves prove that the pairs
line up; @sec-fasta-fastq shows how to check.
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 2. Would it fit?** Fill in your column of @tbl-my-computer.
Would an uncompressed 30-million-read mate file (about 7.7 GB) fit in your
RAM *if a program loaded all of it at once*, leaving room for the system
and your other programs?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
It depends on your laptop: with 8 GB of RAM, no; with 32 GB, yes. But the
count from step 6 never loads the file: it streams through it, so it works
on any laptop. Some tools do need that much memory or more, which is one
reason to use a cluster.
:::
:::

::: {.check}
**Exercise 3. How long would it take?** Time the line count:

```{.bash filename="Terminal (laptop)"}
time gunzip -c SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | wc -l
```

Find the elapsed time: the `real` line in bash, or the number before
`total` in zsh. Estimate the time for a 30-million-read mate file (600
times larger), then name two reasons the real time could differ from your
estimate.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answer
On the example laptop the count took 0.03 seconds, so 600 times that is
about 20 seconds. Two reasons it could differ: for a file this small, the
time is mostly spent starting the programs, and the file may already be in
memory from step 5, so the small run is not a fair sample. And a big file
may sit on a slower disk or a network filesystem, which makes reading it
the limit. Measuring what limits a job is part of @sec-hpc-slurm and @sec-performance.
:::
:::

## Further reading {#sec-orientation-reading}

- @shotts2025linux, *The Linux Command Line*, chapters 1–3 --- a free,
  gentle book on what a shell and a terminal are; a second explanation of
  this chapter and a preview of Part II.
- @wilson2019swcarpentry, Software Carpentry's [*The Unix
  Shell*](https://swcarpentry.github.io/shell-novice/), the introduction
  episode --- the same ideas taught as a workshop lesson, with exercises.
- @microsoft2025install --- the official, current steps for installing WSL,
  if anything in the Windows tab has changed.
- @wu2018repression --- the study our yeast reads come from; read the
  summary to see what experiment the running dataset measures.
